paper_title: MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $π_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.

sections.content: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments, operations, and interactions (Driess et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025). This expansion brings together heterogeneous perceptual and control demands within shared model. Such diversity arises not only across tasks but also within single interaction: placing an object in tray involves approaching it, establishing contact, transporting it, and positioning it precisely. These operations require different visual cues and control behaviors, often under an unchanged instruction. As environmental and operational coverage expands, central challenge is how shared model can effectively accommodate these heterogeneous demands. Visionlanguageaction (VLA) models provide promising foundation by combining pretrained multimodal representations with action prediction (Brohan et al., 2023a; Kim et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). However, conventional VLA policies execute diverse interactions using shared, static parameter configuration. Context changes their activations and predicted actions, but their effective weights remain fixed, including after full fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation (Hu et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2025a). Different operations must therefore be learned through shared parameters, even when their training signals favor competing updatesa source of interference in joint optimization (Yu et al., 2020a). This raises the question of how effectively shared parameters reconcile the demands of different operations. 1Morph, rooted in Greek morphe (form), means to transform. 1 MorphAct Figure 1: Robot policies morph with changing interaction contexts. (a) single manipulation task involves operations with different perceptual and control demands. (b) Existing robot policies use one fixed parameter configuration across contexts, requiring shared parameters to reconcile competing demands. (c) MorphAct generates context-dependent updates for the visionlanguage and action modules, dynamically adjusting policy parameters as interactions unfold. We investigate this question through operation-level diagnostics using demonstrations from the 65 atomic tasks in RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026). At common policy checkpoint, we examine gradient alignment, the effect of single update on other tasks, and the contributions of individual parameter groups. The diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both the visionlanguage and action modules. Every measured source-improving update also increases loss on batches from other tasks, while opposing parameter-group contributions can cancel within module. These findings expose local adaptation trade-offs in shared parameter space. They motivate shared parameter-generation mechanism whose outputs vary with the interaction context. To address this challenge, we introduce MorphAct, contextual parameterization framework that enables robot policies to morph with changing interaction contexts (Figure 1). MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank parameter updates for the visionlanguage and action modules, allowing shared policy to adjust its effective weights to the current interaction. Because visionlanguage adaptation changes the representations used for control, MorphAct couples the two generators by conditioning action-side parameter generation on the adapted representations. Both generators learn jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. Low-rank factors provide an efficient implementation of these contextual updates. We evaluate MorphAct on X-VLA, π0, and π0.5 (Zheng et al., 2026; Black et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) using LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020b), comparing each backbones baseline with MorphAct. Across the three backbones, MorphAct improves Meta-World average success by 7.5716.30%; on LIBERO, X-VLA, π0, and π0.5 gain 4.15%, 2.50%, and 1.75%, respectively. Real-world evaluation with π0.5 further yields gains of 8.0014.00% across four manipulation tasks. Controlled X-VLA ablations on LIBERO show that fixed generation conditions, single-module adaptation, and action-side generation conditioned on pre-adaptation features each reduce mean success. These results support contextual parameterization and representation coupling for accommodating diverse manipulation demands. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We identify parameter conflicts as challenge to scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions through operation-level diagnostic experiments. (2) We introduce MorphAct, whose representation-coupled generators produce context-dependent visionlanguage and action parameter updates and learn jointly through the native action objective. (3) We demonstrate success gains on three VLA backbones, two simulation benchmarks, and four real-world tasks, with ablations supporting contextual generation and representation coupling.

sections.title: 2 PARAMETER CONFLICTS ACROSS OPERATIONS
sections.content: As robot learning expands across environments and interactions, static-parameter policies must reconcile diverse operational demands through the same weights. We examine whether different 2 MorphAct Figure 2: Parameter conflicts across operations and within modules. (a) Negative-gradient-cosine frequency within and across tasks. (b) Number of other tasks with increased target-batch loss after source update. All 260 updates reduce source-batch loss; dots represent updates and ticks mark round medians. (c) Fraction of absolute alignment contribution cancelled across parameter groups within each module. Measurements use one checkpoint with 16 sampling rounds for (a,c) and four for (b). operations favor compatible changes to these parameters. Our diagnostics measure gradient alignment, one-step cross-task loss changes, and parameter-group contributions in both visionlanguage and action modules at common checkpoint. Setup. We use demonstrations from the 65 atomic tasks in RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), grouped by native task ID. All measurements use fixed RoboCasa-pretrained π0.5 checkpoint and the native action loss over the full visionlanguage (VLM) and action parameter sets. Each sampling round draws batches Ui and Vi from disjoint episodes of task i. Gradient comparisons use (Ui, Uj) across tasks and (Ui, Vi) as within-task reference. For one-step transfer, Ui supplies the update and Vj the target evaluation. Appendix details sampling, numerical settings, and metrics. 2.1 CONFLICTING DIRECTIONS IN BOTH MODULES We first ask whether different tasks favor compatible parameter changes. At the common checkpoint, we compute task-batch gradients separately for the VLM and action modules and compare their cosine similarity. negative cosine indicates competing local descent directions (Yu et al., 2020a). Across 16 sampling rounds, negative alignment occurs in 47.80% of cross-task VLM comparisons and 48.28% of action comparisons, versus 38.94% and 42.69% within tasks (Figure 2(a)). The within-task reference shows that update directions also vary among episodes of the same task, while cross-task comparisons produce negative alignment more frequently. Competing adaptation demands therefore affect both the representations used for control and the action mapping. 2.2 CROSS-TASK INTERFERENCE FROM PARAMETER UPDATES Gradient alignment describes local update directions; we next measure the loss changes produced by an actual update. For each source batch Ui, we take one full-parameter gradient step and evaluate the target batches Vj, restarting from the common checkpoint for every source. Target observations, action targets, flow times, and noise remain fixed before and after the step. Across four rounds, all 260 updates reduce their source-batch loss, with mean relative reduction of 2.38%. Yet each update increases loss on batches from 2246 of the other 64 tasks, with median of 32 (Figure 2(b)). Every source-improving update thus has both helpful and harmful effects on other tasks: improving the source does not produce uniformly beneficial transfer across manipulation contexts. 2.3 CONFLICTING CONTRIBUTIONS ACROSS PARAMETER GROUPS The preceding comparisons summarize each module as whole. To examine the interactions within these summaries, we decompose gradient alignment across 47 VLM groups and 19 action groups, 3 MorphAct Figure 3: Representation-coupled parameter generation. Gv generates visionlanguage updates from multimodal embeddings. The adapted VLM pass produces ht for action-side parameter generation and Ct for native action conditioning. Ga generates action updates from ht and robot state. Solid arrows carry data; dashed arrows inject updates. Both generators learn through the action objective, and their outputs are reused within each action chunk. including individual Transformer blocks (Shi et al., 2023). Each groups gradient inner product is normalized by the same full-module gradient norms, so the contributions sum to the module-level cosine. Positive and negative contributions can offset one another. We sum the absolute contribution mass canceled within each pair and divide by the total absolute contribution mass across comparisons. For cross-task pairs, cancellation reaches 36.13% in the VLM and 30.90% in the action module, compared with 23.51% and 22.70% within tasks (Figure 2(c)). small module-level cosine can therefore reflect opposing parameter-group contributions rather than uniformly weak interactions. Appendix A.3 reports the complete group definitions and decomposition. Implication for MorphAct. Together, these results show that adaptation demands differ across tasks and act on both representation and action parameters. An update that serves one context can work against another, with opposing contributions hidden by module-level summaries. This motivates sharing the adaptation mechanism while allowing its updates to depend on the current context. MorphAct uses two generators connected by the adapted visuallanguage representation.

sections.title: 3 MORPHACT: MORPH WITH THE ENVIRONMENT AND THEN ACT
sections.content: MorphAct adjusts robot policy parameters to the current interaction context before predicting an action chunk (Figure 3). Two generators produce context-dependent updates for the visionlanguage and action modules, with action-side generation conditioned on the adapted visionlanguage representations. We describe this coupled generation process and its low-rank parameterization, then explain how both generators learn through the native action objective and how their outputs are reused within each action chunk. 3.1 REPRESENTATION-COUPLED GENERATION Let xt = (ot, ℓ, st) denote the observation, instruction, and robot state at replanning time t. We denote the base policy parameters by θ, with visionlanguage and action modules parameterized by θv and θa. MorphAct generates θ(xt) = (θv,t, θa,t) for selected projections and predicts an action chunk as (cid:98)Yt = πθ+θ(xt)(xt), suppressing sampling randomness. The generator weights are shared across contexts, while their outputs determine the context-dependent effective parameters. 4 MorphAct The two updates follow the policys computational dependency: visionlanguage adaptation changes the representations used for control, so action-side generation conditions on the adapted features. Given multimodal embeddings et = E(ot, ℓ), the forward computation is θv,t = Gv(et; ϕv), (ht, Ct) = Fv(et; θv + θv,t), ua,t = Ca(ht, st; ρa), θa,t = Ga(ua,t; ϕa). (1) Here, ht supplies the action generators visuallanguage condition, whereas Ct retains the action modules native conditioning path. Both are outputs of the same adapted VLM pass. In π0 and π0.5, they correspond to final multimodal prefix tokens and layer-wise prefix keyvalue states, respectively. The constructor Ca appends robot-state token projected by ρa to ht. Thus, the generators have separate parameters but are connected through the representation produced by upstream adaptation. Structured low-rank synthesis. Both generators use the structured synthesis primitive of HYWU (Wu et al., 2026), with distinct target layouts for the two modules. Queries encode layer and projection/rank identities; generator blocks combine cross-layer attention, within-layer parameter attention, and cross-attention to the condition tokens. Separate A/B readouts then produce the factors for each selected block. The generators attend to individual condition tokens. For block j, the generated factors are Aj,t Rdin,j rj and Bj,t Rrj dout,j . With scaling coefficient αj, the update and its residual contribution for row-vector input are αj rj (uAj,t)Bj,t. Wj,t = Aj,tBj,t, δyj,t = αj rj (2) The factored computation avoids materializing dense updates. Q/K/V projections use output-head blocks with their actual query and key/value head counts; attention-output projections sum input-head contributions, while feed-forward projections use matrix-level factors. These layouts accommodate the modules different widths and depths. The rank rj is defined per generated block, not for the assembled multi-head projection. Appendix specifies the factor geometry and output budgets. 3.2 LEARNING THROUGH THE ADAPTED REPRESENTATION MorphAct trains both generators jointly through the base policys action objective, using the same adaptation targets as the corresponding LoRA configuration. Let Φ = (ϕv, ϕa, ρa, ψ) denote the generator parameters, state projection, and projector parameters ψ retained as trainable in that configuration. The remaining VLM and action backbone parameters are frozen. Generated factors are differentiable intermediate outputs, not independent optimization variables. For demonstrations (xt, Yt) D, we optimize min Φ E(xt,Yt)D, ξ (cid:2)Lnative (cid:0) (cid:98)yΦ(xt, Yt; ξ), Yt; ξ(cid:1)(cid:3) , (3) where ξ contains the randomness required by the native training objective, and (cid:98)yΦ denotes its trainingtime prediction. For π0 and π0.5, the sampled time and noise ξ = (τ, ϵ) define zτ = τ ϵ + (1 τ )Yt, and the model predicts the velocity ϵYt, rather than the clean inference chunk (cid:98)Yt. This is conditional flow matching along linear actionnoise path (Lipman et al., 2023). The adapted representation participates in learning through two routes: native action conditioning and action-side parameter generation. Writing rt = (ht, Ct) and the per-sample loss as ℓt(rt, θa,t), with other inputs suppressed, the upstream gradient is ϕv ℓt = rt,ϕv (cid:104) ℓt rt + θa,t,rt ℓt θa,t (cid:105) , Jy,z = z . (4) The first term differentiates through action conditioning while holding the action update fixed; the second accounts for the updates dependence on adapted features. Neither route is detached. The action objective therefore trains the upstream generator through both the representations used for control and the parameters generated from those representations. 3.3 CONTEXT-LEVEL ADAPTATION, CHUNK-LEVEL REUSE Action-sequence prediction underlies both ACTs action chunking and Diffusion Policys recedinghorizon control (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023). Parameter generation depends on the current 5 MorphAct observation context, not on noisy actions or internal solver time. At each replanning step, MorphAct generates the VLM update, computes ht and Ct, and generates the action update. These quantities are then reused throughout action-chunk prediction and refreshed at the next replanning observation, without test-time optimization. In π0 and π0.5, the single adapted prefix pass supplies both representation outputs, while the action expert retains its native state and time interfaces, including π0.5s time-conditioned normalization. Appendix provides the inference procedure. 3.4 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Both A/B readouts use small, nonzero weight initialization and zero biases, keeping initial residuals small without blocking gradients to the generator trunk. Generator parameters are stored in FP32, while internal attention and feed-forward layers support BF16 computation. Factor readouts, low-rank products, scaling, and residual accumulation are computed in FP32 before conversion to the backbone output dtype. Training uses AdamW with learning-rate warmup, cosine decay, and global gradient clipping; updates with non-finite losses or gradient norms are skipped. For variable-length conditions, valid tokens are compacted using the supplied masks and grouped by sequence length. The original batch order is restored after generation, preserving gradients through the adapted features. Non-reentrant activation checkpointing reduces training memory. Algorithms 1 and 2 in Appendix provide the complete training and inference procedures, respectively.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate MorphAct on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020b), and four real-world manipulation tasks. These closed-loop evaluations complement the atomic-task analysis in Section 2 by measuring complete task execution. Section 5 examines the contributions of individual design choices through ablations. 4.1 EVALUATION SETTING We use closed-loop task success as the primary metric. In simulation, we compare MorphAct with the corresponding baselines for X-VLA, π0, and π0.5 under the same task settings. On LIBERO, we train jointly on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long (LIBERO-10), each containing ten tasks, and report suite-level success and their arithmetic average as the Mean score. On Meta-World, we train jointly on all 50 tasks in MT50 and report success for four difficulty groups: Easy (28 tasks), Medium (11), Hard (6), and Very Hard (5). Avg. is the unweighted arithmetic mean of the four group success rates. We evaluate 50 rollouts per task on LIBERO and twenty on Meta-World. MorphAct uses execution horizon H10 on LIBERO. On Meta-World, its checkpoint and execution-horizon settings are 20k / H3 for π0, 17.5k / H4 for π0.5, and 82k / H4 for X-VLA. The two main simulation tables report MorphActs mean scores across three random seeds, each using these rollout counts, and the sample variance of the three overall scores in squared percentage points (pp2). Baseline scores are retained from the original comparison; their variances are not reported. For real-world evaluation, we compare π0.5 with and without MorphAct on four manipulation tasks, using 50 physical rollouts per task for each method. Section 4.4 describes the tasks. 4.2 LIBERO Table 1 shows that MorphAct improves mean success on all three backbones. On X-VLA, success rises from 93.05% to 97.20%, gain of 4.15 percentage points. On π0, it increases from 94.15% to 96.65%, gain of 2.50 points. MorphAct also improves π0.5 from 96.85% to 98.60%, adding 1.75 points to the highest baseline mean in this comparison. For π0.5, it improves Object, Goal, and Long, while Spatial changes from 98.80% to 98.33%. Under matched hardware and execution settings, end-to-end chunk latency increases by approximately 18.0021.00% relative to shared LoRA on π0 and π0.5. This measurement covers observation preprocessing and complete action-chunk prediction, including parameter generation and low-rank residual computation. Appendix D.2 reports generator parameter counts, active-factor counts, and measured chunk latency, inference memory, and control rate.

sections.title: 5 ANALYSIS
sections.content: We examine three design choices in MorphAct: the condition used for parameter generation, the modules receiving updates, and the features connecting the two generators. Ablations use X-VLA on LIBERO under the task setup and evaluation protocol in Section 4.1. Table 3 reports success rates, with superscripts linking each variant to the comparisons below. 5.1 CONTEXT BEYOND TASK IDENTITY Comparison varies the generation condition while retaining the policys normal image, language, and robot-state inputs. Constant uses one fixed condition across tasks, whereas Task-ID uses one per task. Both retain MorphActs generators. Task-ID raises mean success from 87.50% to 88.25%, improving Object, Goal, and Long but reducing Spatial by 3.40 percentage points. MorphAct reaches 97.20%, exceeding Constant and Task-ID by 9.70 and 8.95 points on average, with improvements on every suite. The largest gains occur on Long, at 15.60 and 12.20 points, respectively. Both fixed-condition variants trail the X-VLA baselines 93.05% mean success in Table 1, by 5.55 and 8 MorphAct 4.80 points. MorphAct instead lets updates respond to the current observation and robot state. The comparison supports contextual generation beyond assigning fixed update to each task. 5.2 ADAPTING BOTH MODULES Comparison examines the contribution of each adapted module. VLM-only and Action-only disable generated updates in the other module but retain both modules in the policy. Action-only achieves 81.00% mean success versus 43.50% for VLM-only, making action-side generation the stronger single-module choice. We then compare Action-only with Unadapted to separate upstream adaptation from feature coupling. Both use pre-adaptation features to condition the action generator. Unadapted additionally adapts the representation supplied to the action predictor, raising mean success from 81.00% to 86.00% with improvements on all four suites. Upstream adaptation thus benefits action prediction even when its output does not condition action updates. 5.3 COUPLING THROUGH ADAPTED FEATURES Comparison tests the features supplied to the action generator. Unadapted and MorphAct both generate updates for both modules and use adapted features for action prediction. Unadapted conditions action-side generation on pre-adaptation features, while MorphAct uses the adapted VLM output. This raises mean success from 86.00% to 97.20%, gain of 11.20 percentage points. The suite-level results distinguish this effect from upstream adaptation alone. On Object, adding VLM updates raises success from Action-onlys 92.00% to Unadapteds 97.80%, and coupling adds another 2.07 points. On Long, upstream adaptation adds 2.20 points, while coupling adds 21.60 points. Coupling also improves Goal by 13.47 points. Both feature sources support high success on Object, but Goal and Long benefit more from generating action updates that respond to the representation produced by upstream adaptation. Summary. The ablations support current-context conditioning, adaptation of both modules, and coupling through adapted VLM features. Task identity alone provides small average gain over constant conditioning, whereas current-context generation improves all four suites. The progression from Action-only to Unadapted to MorphAct separates the benefit of adapting the representation from the further benefit of using it to generate action updates. Together, these comparisons show that parameter generation depends on both the current context and the adapted features used for control.

sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: VLA models. Generalist robot policies scale learning across tasks and embodiments (Brohan et al., 2023b; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024), while Octo supports adaptation to new observation and action spaces (Ghosh et al., 2024). VIMA specifies manipulation tasks through interleaved textual and visual prompts (Jiang et al., 2023). RT-2, OpenVLA, and the π family connect pretrained visionlanguage representations to robot actions (Brohan et al., 2023a; Kim et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). MorphAct studies how representation and action modules can adapt to changing manipulation contexts within shared policy. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Adapters and prefix-tuning learn small task-specific components while freezing pretrained weights (Houlsby et al., 2019; Li & Liang, 2021). LoRA learns low-rank weight updates (Hu et al., 2022), and DoRA separates weight magnitude and direction, applying low-rank adaptation to the latter (Liu et al., 2024). For VLA models, OpenVLA-OFT studies efficient decoding and fine-tuning objectives (Kim et al., 2025a), X-VLA uses embodiment-specific soft prompts (Zheng et al., 2026), and VLA-Adapter introduces Bridge Attention between visionlanguage features and lightweight action policy (Wang et al., 2026a). MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank updates while retaining the host policys action interface and objective. Parameter sharing and generation. Multi-task learning studies structural sharing (Yang et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2022), joint optimization (Sener & Koltun, 2018; Chen et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2020a; Liu et al., 2021), and task transfer and layerwise conflicts (Fifty et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2023). Parameter generation synthesizes network weights using hypernetworks (Ha et al., 2017) or diffusion models (Wang et al., 2024; 2025), treating weights as generative modality (Wang et al., 2026b) and enabling adaptation conditioned on tasks, features, examples, images, or prompts (Karimi Mahabadi et al., 9 MorphAct 2021; Ivison & Peters, 2022; Phang et al., 2023; Ruiz et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025). HY-WU studies structured synthesis of low-rank weight updates (Wu et al., 2026). Hyper-LoRA generates instruction-conditioned updates (Xiong et al., 2024), HyperVLA generates compact-policy parameters once per episode for efficient inference (Xiong et al., 2025), and PhaseLoRA modulates action-side LoRA per chunk (Guo et al., 2026). MorphAct couples parameter generation across perception and action: adapted visionlanguage representations condition action-side parameter updates, and both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank updates for visionlanguage and action modules through shared adaptation mechanism. Its generators are coupled through adapted representations and trained jointly with the native action objective. Atomic-task diagnostics reveal conflicting adaptation demands in both modules, while evaluations on LIBERO, Meta-World, and four realworld tasks demonstrate improved closed-loop manipulation. Ablations further support contextual generation, adaptation of both modules, and coupling through adapted VLM features.

The VLM diagnostic set contains 2,923,335,408 scalar parameters, and the action set contains 430,098,464. sections.title: C JOINT TRAINING AND POLICY EXECUTION
sections.content: Algorithms 1 and 2 summarize one training update and action-chunk prediction at one replanning context. Both follow the generation order in Equation (1): generate the VLM update, compute the adapted representation, and generate the action update. Generated updates are applied as low-rank residuals, without materializing dense weight updates. Only Φ = (ϕv, ϕa, ρa, ψ) is optimized, where ψ denotes the projector parameters retained as trainable by the adaptation configuration. The remaining backbone parameters stay frozen. The condition constructor Ca uses adapted features and robot state; for X-VLA, it additionally includes native auxiliary-view features. Training evaluates per-context operations over the demonstration batch. Both A/B readout weights are initialized from zero-mean Gaussian with standard deviation σ0/(cid:112)dg and zero bias, where dg is the readout input width. The generated residual δy = (α/r)uAB obeys δy2 (α/r)u2A2B2, using spectral norms for the factors. Small factor scales thus favor small local residuals, without imposing an exactly zero initial policy update. If an entire factor readout is initialized to zero, the generator trunk initially receives no gradient through that product: one factor derivative is multiplied by zero, while the zero readout has zero input Jacobian. Small, nonzero weights on both readouts avoid this structural blockage. Precision and optimization. Generator parameters are stored in FP32; internal attention and feedforward computation can use BF16. Factor readouts, low-rank multiplications, scaling, and residual accumulation are evaluated in FP32 before conversion to the base output dtype. The conversion can still quantize sufficiently small residual. The training implementation uses one AdamW schedule with warmup and cosine decay, global gradient clipping, and checks that prevent updates on non-finite losses or gradient norms. The π implementation additionally checks trainable-gradient coverage. Non-reentrant activation checkpointing reduces activation memory. Variable-length conditioning. Valid condition tokens are compacted using the supplied masks, grouped by sequence length, and restored to the original batch order after generation. Token compaction and reordering preserve gradients to the condition features. Grouping can require separate generator invocations for different sequence lengths within batch; generated updates are reused per observation and action chunk. sections.title: D ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: D.1 ABLATION CONFIGURATIONS The variants in Table 3 examine conditioning, adaptation targets, and the representation passed between generators. Task-ID assigns fixed generation condition to each task, while Constant uses conditions that remain fixed across tasks and observations. Both variants retain the policys normal image, language, and robot-state inputs. VLM-only disables generated action-side updates; Actiononly disables generated VLM updates while retaining visual inputs. Unadapted keeps both generators active but feeds the action generator the VLM representation computed before the generated VLM update. The action predictor continues to receive the adapted representation, so this variant specifically changes the condition used for action-side parameter generation. D.2 ADAPTATION BUDGET AND RUNTIME For Nsolve action-refinement steps, the approximate computation is Tpolicy TE + TGv + TFv + TGa + NsolveTFa . Generator costs include condition construction, and adapted-module costs include the generated residuals. Generation is paid per context rather than per solver step. Contextual parameterization separates learned generator weights from the updates instantiated for an observation. We report the parameter count of the two generators and, separately, the number of scalar A/B entries in an active low-rank update. Shared LoRA reuses learned factors across contexts, whereas MorphAct generates them from the current context; generated factors are outputs, not additional independently optimized parameters. Explicit factor counts also account for differences between head-aware and matrix-level layouts that nominal rank alone does not capture. Table A8 pairs these counts with end-to-end chunk latency, measured inference memory, and control rate. Timing covers observation preprocessing and complete action-chunk prediction, including parameter generation and residual computation where applicable. Methods are compared on matched hardware and execution settings, including solver steps, predicted action horizon, and executed-prefix length. Control rate is measured under the actual action-execution schedule, rather than inferred solely from the inverse of chunk-prediction latency. Adaptation Backbone: π0 Shared LoRA MorphAct Backbone: π0.5 Shared LoRA MorphAct Generator params (M) Active factors (M) Chunk latency (ms) Memory (GiB) 300.09 300.09 49.99 49.99 49.99 49.99 120.00 145. 138.71 164.00 7.43 9.10 7.88 9.53 Rate (Hz) 28.09 23.20 24.99 21. Table A8: Adaptation capacity and execution cost. Generator counts include the two generators only; indicates the absence of generator. Active factors count scalar A/B entries used by one context, not the number of matrices. Execution measurements use matched settings within each backbone. Control rates are measured under the action-execution schedule. MorphAct reuses the generated updates throughout action-chunk prediction, keeping parameter generation outside the solver loop. This amortizes generation across refinement steps but retains the cost of computing and applying the updates. Relative to shared LoRA, chunk latency rises by 25.00 ms on π0 and 25.29 ms on π0.5, while inference memory rises by 1.67 and 1.65 GiB, respectively. Measured control rates are 23.20 and 21.20 Hz for MorphAct, compared with 28.09 and 24.99 Hz for shared LoRA. Read together with Table 1, these measurements characterize the manipulation-performanceexecution-cost trade-off of contextual adaptation.
